state.description:
Every test this strategy will not bend has passed, enough of the rest have, and you have answered the three questions no filing can answer with a yes.

subject.label: Return on invested capital, 5-year median
subject.explain:
How many cents of profit the business earns per dollar that's tied up
in it. A company earning 20 cents on every dollar of capital is a
machine; one earning 7 cents is a job.

threshold_from.label: Lowest return on invested capital

subject.label: Total debt to average free cash flow, 5-year
subject.explain:
How many years of the cash the business actually generates it would
take to repay everything it owes. At 3 it would take three years of
every spare dollar.

It asks the same question as debt against EBITDA and answers it with a
number the company cannot present its way out of. EBITDA adds back
depreciation, which is the cost of the equipment wearing out;
free cash flow has already paid for replacing it. For a business that
needs a lot of machinery, the two figures can differ by half.

threshold_from.label: Highest debt against the cash it generates

subject.label: Owner earnings yield on enterprise value
subject.explain:
The cash the business throws off for its owners each year, divided by
what the whole business costs — the shares AND the debts that come
with them.

It differs from the plainer owner earnings yield in two ways, and both
of them make the answer smaller for the companies that were being
flattered.

The price is the enterprise value. Owner earnings is a figure about
the business, and buying a business with borrowings attached means
taking on the borrowings; priced against the shares alone, a heavily
indebted company looks cheap precisely for being indebted.

And the maintenance-capex proxy leaves out the amortization of
intangibles. The proxy works on the reasoning that a business
replacing its equipment spends about what it writes it down by. A
customer list bought in an acquisition is written down over ten years
and is never replaced by spending — it is replaced by another
acquisition. Counting it raises the floor of the proxy, so it
subtracts less, so owner earnings come out higher — and they come out
highest for the serial acquirers where the reasoning holds least.

threshold_from.label: Lowest owner earnings yield

subject.label: Incremental return on invested capital, 5-year
subject.explain:
What the money the company kept has earned — as opposed to what the
money already in the business earns.

Return on invested capital describes the existing base: everything
built, bought and borrowed over the company's whole life, taken
together. This describes only the increment. Profit is higher than it
was five years ago by some amount; the capital tied up in the business
is higher by some amount; the first divided by the second is what the
retained profits bought.

It is the number that decides how fast a business compounds. A company
earning 30% on its existing base and 6% on everything new is a company
that has run out of places to put money, and the 30% will drift down
toward the 6% for as long as it keeps reinvesting. The base tells you
what was built. This tells you what is being built now.

threshold_from.label: Lowest return on the money it keeps

subject.label: Interest coverage
subject.explain:
How many times over the company's operating profit covers its interest
bill. At 8x, earnings could fall by half and the lenders still get paid
without anyone noticing.

threshold_from.label: Lowest interest coverage

subject.label: Return on equity above return on invested capital, 5-year
subject.explain:
Return on equity counts only the owners' money. Return on invested
capital counts the borrowed money too. So the distance between them is
borrowing, and nothing else: a company earning 30% on its owners'
money and 12% on all the money in the business is producing most of
that 30% with debt rather than with the business.

A wide gap is not a fraud and not always a mistake. It is a statement
that the returns being admired belong partly to the lenders, and that
they get thinner the moment borrowing gets dearer or harder.

threshold_from.label: Most of the return that may be borrowed

subject.label: Free cash flow margin, 5-year median
subject.explain:
Out of every hundred dollars of sales, how many end up as spendable
cash after keeping the lights on and the equipment current. Ten dollars
is healthy. Zero means the business grows by consuming everything it
earns.

threshold_from.label: Lowest free cash flow margin

subject.label: Cash conversion, 5-year median
subject.explain:
Whether the reported profits turn into actual money. If a company
reports a billion in earnings and collects nine hundred million in cash,
fine. If it reports a billion and collects three hundred million, the
earnings are an accounting opinion. Persistently below 0.80 means
accruals, aggressive capitalisation, or receivables that aren't being
collected.

threshold_from.label: Lowest cash conversion

subject.label: Revenue CAGR, 5-year
subject.explain:
How fast sales have grown per year over five years. Roughly, whether the
business is growing at least as fast as the economy around it — nominal
GDP growth is the natural yardstick.

threshold_from.label: Lowest revenue growth

subject.label: Net income CAGR minus revenue CAGR, 5-year
subject.explain:
Whether profits are growing at least as fast as sales. If sales grow 8%
and profits grow 3%, the company is buying its growth by giving away
margin.

threshold_from.label: Lowest gap between profit growth and sales growth

subject.label: Gross margin range as a share of the margin, 5-year
subject.explain:
The same question as the plain range — does this company set its own
prices, or does the market set them — asked in a way that means the
same thing at any margin.

A distributor earning 12% and swinging between 9% and 15% moved six
points, and half its margin came and went. A software company earning
81% and swinging between 78% and 84% also moved six points, and barely
noticed. The first is a commodity business; the second sets its own
prices. Measured in points they are identical, which is the problem.
Measured against the margin itself, the first reads 50% and the second
7%.

threshold_from.label: Widest the gross margin may swing, against its own size

subject.label: Diluted share count change, 5-year
subject.explain:
Whether your slice of the company is getting bigger or smaller. A
company can grow earnings 8% a year and still deliver you nothing if it
issues 8% more shares a year. Stock compensation is a real expense that
transfers ownership from you to employees quietly.

threshold_from.label: Most the share count may grow

subject.label: Goodwill written off over five years, against opening equity
subject.explain:
How much of what the company paid for other businesses it has since
admitted was not there — measured against the owners' money that
existed before the write-offs began.

Goodwill is the premium an acquirer pays over what the acquired
company's identifiable assets are worth. Writing it off is management
conceding, in public and in the accounts, that the premium bought
nothing. One write-off is a deal that went wrong. A run of them
against a large share of the equity base is a company whose growth has
been purchased at prices it could not justify.

The denominator is the equity BEFORE the window rather than after it,
and that is deliberate: impairments reduce equity, so measuring
against today's would divide a large numerator by a denominator the
same charges had already shrunk, and flatter the worst cases most.

threshold_from.label: Most of the owners' money that may have been written off

subject.label: Total debt to EBITDA
subject.explain:
How many years of earnings it would take to repay everything the
company owes. Two years is comfortable. Five is a company whose future
belongs partly to its lenders.

threshold_from.label: Highest debt against earnings before depreciation

subject.label: Moat durability
subject.explain:
A moat is whatever makes it hard or unprofitable for someone else to do
what this company does — a brand people ask for by name, a network that
gets more useful as it grows, a cost position nobody can match, a
switching cost customers won't pay. The question is not whether the
company is winning now. It is whether the reason it is winning will
still hold.

subject.label: Capital allocation
subject.explain:
Every year a company decides what to do with the money it earns:
reinvest it, buy something, pay down debt, buy back stock, or hand it
over. Done well this compounds; done badly it is the main way good
businesses become ordinary ones. The distinction to look for is whether
the chief executive behaves like an allocator of capital or like an
empire builder.

subject.label: Names held at once
subject.explain:
How many separate companies this strategy holds at one time. Each first purchase takes an equal share of the account, so ten names means about ten percent each, and once every place is taken a new candidate is told there is no room rather than being talked down.

Ten is the top of Buffett's own stated range. His 1993 letter to shareholders argues that an investor who can identify five to ten sensibly-priced companies with durable advantages has no use for conventional diversification. The top of that range is used rather than the bottom because five names is a concentration somebody should arrive at deliberately, having done the work, and not one a tool should hand them by default.

Move toward five and every position doubles in consequence — including the one where your assessment of the moat turns out to be wrong, which is the risk this style carries and Graham's does not. Move past twenty and you are holding more businesses than anyone can follow closely enough to answer this strategy's own three questions honestly, which quietly turns the whole method into guessing.

This figure and the position cap below are the only two here that do not come from the expert report — it was never asked about sizing.

subject.label: Most this will put into one name
subject.explain:
The largest share of your account this strategy will take a single holding up to by buying more of it.

**Read what that does and does not mean, because it is the one setting here most likely to be misunderstood.** It is a limit on your purchases, not on the position. If a holding compounds until it is sixty percent of the account, nothing here tells you to trim it — this strategy has no trim, on purpose. What this number does is stop you *adding* past forty percent. The market may take a position wherever it likes; you may not.

Forty percent is Buffett's own figure from his 1965 partnership letter, where he set it as the most he would commit to a single holding, and only in an exceptional case. It is the most concentrated setting in this program by a wide margin, and it is only reachable through repeated purchases, each of which has to pass every entry test and all three of your own assessments on the day it is made.

It is deliberately far above the ten percent a first purchase is sized at. The gap between the two is where this strategy differs from a rebalancing one: money is added to what keeps proving itself rather than moved back toward an average.

It needs this journal's cash record to be open, because a share of the account cannot be worked out without knowing what the account is. Until it is, the size rules report that they could not be run.

Attributed to Buffett's practice, not to the expert report, which does not cover sizing.

subject.label: Names held at once
subject.explain:
How many separate companies this strategy holds at one time. Each first purchase takes an equal share of the account, so ten names means about ten percent each, and once every place is taken a new candidate is told there is no room rather than being talked down.

Ten is the top of Buffett's own stated range. His 1993 letter to shareholders argues that an investor who can identify five to ten sensibly-priced companies with durable advantages has no use for conventional diversification. The top of that range is used rather than the bottom because five names is a concentration somebody should arrive at deliberately, having done the work, and not one a tool should hand them by default.

Move toward five and every position doubles in consequence — including the one where your assessment of the moat turns out to be wrong, which is the risk this style carries and Graham's does not. Move past twenty and you are holding more businesses than anyone can follow closely enough to answer this strategy's own three questions honestly, which quietly turns the whole method into guessing.

This figure and the position cap below are the only two here that do not come from the expert report — it was never asked about sizing.

subject.label: Most this will put into one name
subject.explain:
The largest share of your account this strategy will take a single holding up to by buying more of it.

**Read what that does and does not mean, because it is the one setting here most likely to be misunderstood.** It is a limit on your purchases, not on the position. If a holding compounds until it is sixty percent of the account, nothing here tells you to trim it — this strategy has no trim, on purpose. What this number does is stop you *adding* past forty percent. The market may take a position wherever it likes; you may not.

Forty percent is Buffett's own figure from his 1965 partnership letter, where he set it as the most he would commit to a single holding, and only in an exceptional case. It is the most concentrated setting in this program by a wide margin, and it is only reachable through repeated purchases, each of which has to pass every entry test and all three of your own assessments on the day it is made.

It is deliberately far above the ten percent a first purchase is sized at. The gap between the two is where this strategy differs from a rebalancing one: money is added to what keeps proving itself rather than moved back toward an average.

It needs this journal's cash record to be open, because a share of the account cannot be worked out without knowing what the account is. Until it is, the size rules report that they could not be run.

subject.label: Names held at once
subject.explain:

His 1993 letter to shareholders argues that an investor who can identify five to ten sensibly-priced companies with durable advantages has no use for conventional diversification. The top of that range is used rather than the bottom because five names is a concentration somebody should arrive at deliberately, having done the work, and not one a tool should hand them by default.

subject.label: Names held at once
subject.explain:
How many separate companies this strategy holds at one time. Each first purchase takes an equal share of the account, so ten names means about ten percent each, and once every place is taken a new candidate is told there is no room rather than being talked down.

Ten is the top of Buffett's own stated range. His 1993 letter to shareholders argues that an investor who can identify five to ten sensibly-priced companies with durable advantages has no use for conventional diversification. The top of that range is used rather than the bottom because five names is a concentration somebody should arrive at deliberately, having done the work, and not one a tool should hand them by default.

Move toward five and every position doubles in consequence — including the one where your assessment of the moat turns out to be wrong, which is the risk this style carries and Graham's does not. Move past twenty and you are holding more businesses than anyone can follow closely enough to answer this strategy's own three questions honestly, which quietly turns the whole method into guessing.

This figure and the position cap below are the only two here that do not come from the expert report — it was never asked about sizing.

subject.label: Most this will put into one name
subject.explain:
The largest share of your account this strategy will take a single holding up to by buying more of it.

**Read what that does and does not mean, because it is the one setting here most likely to be misunderstood.** It is a limit on your purchases, not on the position. If a holding compounds until it is sixty percent of the account, nothing here tells you to trim it — this strategy has no trim, on purpose. What this number does is stop you *adding* past forty percent. The market may take a position wherever it likes; you may not.

Forty percent is Buffett's own figure from his 1965 partnership letter, where he set it as the most he would commit to a single holding, and only in an exceptional case. It is the most concentrated setting in this program by a wide margin, and it is only reachable through repeated purchases, each of which has to pass every entry test and all three of your own assessments on the day it is made.

It is deliberately far above the ten percent a first purchase is sized at. The gap between the two is where this strategy differs from a rebalancing one: money is added to what keeps proving itself rather than moved back toward an average.

It needs this journal's cash record to be open, because a share of the account cannot be worked out without knowing what the account is. Until it is, the size rules report that they could not be run.
